title: Partition a whole into equal parts; name the numerator and denominator

lesson.title: Equal Parts: Meet the Top and Bottom Numbers

steps.say: You already know how to share fairly — like cutting a pizza so everyone gets the same amount. Today we learn how to write down that fair share as a fraction, using two numbers with a special job.

visual.caption: One whole pizza, cut into 4 equal slices

steps.say: Here is the big idea. First we cut the whole into equal parts — parts that are exactly the same size. The pizza is cut into four equal slices, so we write four on the bottom. That bottom number is called the denominator, and it tells us how many equal parts the whole was cut into. You took one slice, so we write one on top. That top number is called the numerator, and it counts how many of those parts you have. One out of four equal parts is one fourth.

visual.caption: 1 shaded of 4 equal slices — numerator 1 on top, denominator 4 on the bottom

steps.say: Let us try it with a granola bar from your lunch. Snap it into eight equal pieces. Eight equal pieces means the denominator is eight. You eat three of them, so the numerator is three. You ate three eighths of the granola bar. Notice the bottom number never changes just because you ate some — the bar is still made of eight equal pieces.

visual.caption: 3 of 8 equal pieces eaten — three eighths

steps.say: Now here is a mistake I see a lot, so let us catch it together. Imagine I cut a pizza into four pieces, but one piece is huge and the others are tiny. Someone takes a tiny piece and says, I got one fourth! But that is not true. A fraction only works when every part is the same size. If the pieces are not equal, we cannot call any of them one fourth — it is just a piece, and it has no fraction name at all. So before you write a fraction, always ask yourself: are all the parts the same size?

visual.caption: This one really is one fourth — because all 4 slices are the same size

steps.say: So remember the two jobs. The bottom number, the denominator, tells you how many equal parts the whole was cut into. The top number, the numerator, tells you how many of those parts you are talking about. Equal parts first, then count.
steps.math: \frac{\text{parts you have}}{\text{equal parts in the whole}}

lesson.answer: Cut the whole into equal parts: the bottom number counts the equal parts, the top number counts the ones you have.

practice.question: Ms. Yuanyuan buys a long fruit bar at the store for two dollars and snaps it into 6 equal pieces — picture it as a fraction bar with 6 equal boxes in a row. She shares 4 of those pieces with her friends. Draw the bar yourself and shade 4 boxes. What fraction did she share? Which number is the numerator, and which is the denominator? And here is the tricky part: if she had snapped the bar into 6 pieces that were NOT all the same size, could she still call 4 pieces four sixths?
practice.answer: She shared four sixths of the bar. The numerator is 4 (the pieces she shared) and the denominator is 6 (the equal pieces in the whole bar). No — if the 6 pieces were not the same size, it would not be four sixths at all, because a fraction only works when the parts are equal.
